'''William Jason Morgan''' (October 10, 1935 – July 31, 2023) was an American [[geophysicist]] who made seminal contributions to the theory of [[plate tectonics]] and [[geodynamics]]. He retired as the Knox Taylor Professor [[:wikt:emeritus|emeritus]] of geology and professor of geosciences at [[Princeton University]].<ref>{{Cite journal |editor1=Bill Bonini |editor2=Laurie Wanat |date=Fall 2003 |title=Jason Morgan Retires |url=http://www.princeton.edu/geosciences/about/publications/smilodon/SmiloFall03.pdf |journal=The Smilodon: The Princeton Geosciences Newsletter |volume=44 |issue=2}} Passages about W. Jason Morgan from:
* {{Cite book |last=McPhee |first=John |year=1998 |title=Annals of the Former World |location=New York |publisher=Farrar, Straus, Giroux}}</ref> He served as a [[visiting scholar]] in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at [[Harvard University]] until his death.

== Early life and education ==
Morgan was born on October 10, 1935, in Savannah, Georgia. His father William owned a hardware and dry goods store and his mother Maxie Ponita (Donehoo) Morgan was a French teacher and volunteered with the Girl Scouts of America.<ref name="auto">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/08/11/science/jason-morgan-dead.html|title=W. Jason Morgan, Who Developed Theory of Plate Tectonics, Dies at 87|work=The New York Times |date=August 11, 2023 |last1=Risen |first1=Clay }}</ref>

He attended [[Georgia Institute of Technology]], initially studying mechanical engineering, but switched to physics halfway through his studies. He graduated in 1957. He was in the Navy for two years working as an instructor at its [[Nuclear Power School]], which directed him toward graduate studies. In 1959, he went to Princeton University, where he completed his PhD in 1964 under the supervision of [[Robert H. Dicke]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Simons |first1=Frederik J |title=W. Jason Morgan (Obituary) |journal=Physics Today |date=2023 |issue=December |pages=52 |doi=10.1063/PT.3.5365 |url=https://pubs.aip.org/physicstoday/article/76/12/52/2923596/W-Jason-Morgan|url-access=subscription }}</ref> He joined the faculty of the university immediately afterwards.<ref name="auto"/>

Morgan's Ph.D. thesis about fluctuations in the [[gravitational constant]] was unrelated to geology. As a post-doctoral fellow, he shared an office with the English geologist [[Fred Vine]] who had discovered the bilateral symmetry of [[seafloor spreading]]. After reading [[Henry William Menard|H.W. Menard]]'s work he began to consider how great faults and fracture zones might relate to the geometry of spheres.<ref>{{cite web |title=Plates and Plumes: A Celebration of the Contributions of W. Jason Morgan to the Ongoing Revolution in Earth Dynamics |url=https://geosciences.princeton.edu/sites/g/files/toruqf2391/files/about/publications/morganfest.pdf}}</ref>

==Career==
His first major contribution, made in the late 1960s, was to relate the magnetic anomalies of alternating polarity, which occur on the ocean bottom at both sides of a [[mid-ocean ridge]], to [[seafloor spreading]] and plate tectonics.

From 1971 on he worked on the further development of the [[Mantle plume|plume theory]] of [[Tuzo Wilson]], which postulates the existence of roughly cylindrical convective upwellings in the Earth's [[Mantle (geology)|mantle]] as an explanation of [[Hotspot (geology)|hotspots]]. Wilson originally applied the concept to [[Hawaii]] and explained the increase in age of the [[seamount]]s of the Hawaii-Emperor chain with increasing distance from the current hotspot location; however, the concept was subsequently applied to many other hotspots by Morgan and other scientists.

"The theory of plate tectonics he published in 1968 is one of the major milestones of U.S. science in the 20th century," [[Francis Anthony Dahlen|F. A. Dahlen]], chair of the Princeton Department of Geosciences, wrote in 2003.<ref>[http://www.princeton.edu/pr/news/03/q4/1022-morgan.htm Princeton geophysicist to receive National Medal of Science]. Princeton University press release (October 22, 2003)</ref>
"Essentially all of the research in solid-earth geophysical sciences in the past 30 to 35 years has been firmly grounded upon Jason Morgan's plate tectonic theory," Dahlen said. "The scientific careers of a generation of geologists and geophysicists have been founded upon his landmark 1968 paper."<ref>{{cite web | url=https://pr.princeton.edu/news/03/q4/1022-morgan.htm | title=Princeton geophysicist to receive National Medal of Science }}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
Morgan received many honors and awards for his work, among them the [[Bucher Medal]] (1972), the [[Alfred Wegener]] Medal of the [[European Geosciences Union]] (1983), the [[Maurice Ewing Medal]] of the [[American Geophysical Union]] (1987), the [[Japan Prize]] (1990), the [[Wollaston Medal]] of the [[Geological Society of London]] (1994)<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.geolsoc.org.uk/gsl/null/lang/en/page750.html|title=Wollaston Medal|work=Award Winners since 1831|publisher=[[Geological Society of London]]|access-date=February 25, 2009|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090321180704/http://www.geolsoc.org.uk/gsl/null/lang/en/page750.html|archive-date=March 21, 2009}}</ref> and the [[National Medal of Science]] of the US, award year 2002.<ref>[[National Science Foundation]], 
[https://www.nsf.gov/od/nms/recip_details.cfm?recip_id=5000000000420 "W. Jason Morgan"], The President's National Medal of Science: Recipient Details.</ref>

==Personal life==
In 1959, Morgan married Cary Goldschmidt. Together they had two children. She died in 1991.<ref name="auto"/> He died in [[Natick, Massachusetts]] on July 31, 2023, at the age of 87.<ref>{{cite web |title=W. Jason Morgan |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/w-jason-morgan-rp8p2n/ |website=National Academy of Sciences |access-date=August 12, 2023}}</ref>
